title: A privilege boundary that chroots still resolves identity from inside the chroot the caller controls
index_line: T-0047 · EXEC · sudo -R enters a user-made tree, then reads nsswitch.conf from it and dlopens the module it names · c · corroborated
invariant_violated: Switching into a chroot is treated as *containment*: the process is fenced, so what it finds inside is the caller's to arrange and nobody else's business. But privilege logic runs *after* the fence goes up — the identity lookups that decide who the caller is resolve through files inside the chroot, and one of those files names a shared library to load, as root.

mechanism.does: a local user builds a directory containing their own `etc/nsswitch.conf` and a shared object it names
the privileged tool is invoked with its chroot option pointed at that directory
the chroot is applied before the identity/policy lookups run, so those lookups resolve inside the caller's tree
the NSS configuration selects the caller's module by path, and the loader opens it with the tool's privileges
the module's initialiser runs as root before any policy decision is reached

source.env.value: a directory the caller owns and can populate — the input is a *filesystem layout*, not a string

fs.path.join.value: chroot-relative resolution: the same path string means one file to the tool and another to the caller

guard.none.value: the ordering itself is the missing guard — resolution happens after the fence, not before it

sink.eval.value: the dynamic loader opening a path named by configuration, with elevated privileges

preconditions.expr: the sudo build is in the affected range (the chroot-option change landed in 1.9.14; fixed in 1.9.17p1)
the sudoers policy permits the chroot option for the invoking user
the caller can create a directory tree and a shared object inside it

success: a local unprivileged user gets a root shell without a password
the process tree shows a module loaded from a path under the user's directory while running as root
the timing is instant — there is no race to win, the ordering is deterministic
failure_like: the build predates the chroot-option change, or the sudoers rule does not permit chroot
the tool drops privileges, or resolves identity before applying the chroot
false_positive: a user who already had a sudo right to the command — check `sudo -l` first
a crash when the module fails to load: the attempt reached the loader, which is the precondition, not the win

hazards: the audit question is ordering: which privileged lookups happen *after* an attacker-influenced context switch (chroot, namespace, cwd, mount)
any chroot/namespace/journal option that takes a path from the caller is a candidate — the fence does not make the contents trusted
NSS, PAM, ld.so.preload and locale modules are all 'configuration that names a library'; each is the same bug with a different file
this is not a race and not an injection: nothing is concatenated, nothing is raced. The defect is sequence
non_transfers: tools that resolve identity before entering the caller-supplied context
builds without the chroot option, or policies that never grant it

evidence.target: sudo 1.9.14–1.9.17 with the chroot option permitted (CVE-2025-32463), fixed 1.9.17p1
